results.note: p. 391 Introduction ¶1 (rendered) says all of this as cited background; 'None of this is tested' is a fair editorial note: the study tests no mechanism.

Dates, place, sexes, ages, follow-up, 17 of 18 admitting use, 7 without reliable history and WG controls match p. 391 and Table 1; the WG follow-up (13–108 months) sits at the top of p. 392, where ¶2 continues.

results.corrected_extracted: All 18 sought care for long-standing symptoms including nasal obstruction, nosebleeds and severe facial pain (facial pain in 3 of 18 by Table 1, p. 392); the commonest findings at the first visit were diffuse necrotising ulcers, extensive crusting and septal perforation; clinically, destruction of the septum and inferior turbinates was found in all (imaging: inferior turbinate in 12 of 16), extending in more severe cases to the middle and superior turbinates and the lateral nasal wall, entirely absorbed in 3; hard and soft palate perforations were present in 2 at the first visit and appeared during follow-up in 3 more. The authors say the lesions gave rise to difficulty swallowing and nasal reflux (numbers not given) and substantially affected quality of life, which was not measured.
results.note: The source says 'The lesions gave rise to dysphagia and nasal reflux', not the palate perforations as such, with no numbers; 'severe' facial pain restored. All else matches p. 393 ¶1.
16 of 18 imaged (CT 5, MRI 11; all read by RM, radiology), counts, percentages, bilateral counts and WG zeros match p. 392 ¶1–2, p. 395 ¶2 and Table 3 (rendered).

results.corrected_extracted: Figure 3 prints, for the lesion group, septum 100%, inferior turbinate 61%, middle turbinate 33%, superior turbinate 16%, lateral wall 11% and floor or palate 28% (septum 12% for Wegener granulomatosis). Except for the septum these do not match the imaging counts in the text and Table 3 (12, 10, 2, 5 and 4 of 16: 75%, 62.5%, 12.5%, 31.25% and 25%), nor the clinical statement that the inferior turbinates were destroyed in all; only the 28% matches a stated count, the 5 of 18 with palate perforations at the first visit or during follow-up (27.8%, p. 393). The values are close to counts of 11, 6, 3, 2 and 5 out of 18 (61.1%, 33.3%, 16.7%, 11.1% and 27.8%; editors' arithmetic), which the paper does not explain. The claim uses the counts of 16 from the text and Table 3.
results.note: Fig. 3 read at 500 dpi: arrows and values as stated. But 28% equals the 5 of 18 palate perforations reported clinically (2 + 3, p. 393), so 'nor the clinical statements' was too broad; 3/18 is 16.7%, not 16%.
p. 392 ¶2 (4 people, n = 8, range 7–52 months), p. 396 ¶8 (all admitted continued use, all progressed; skull base, 'see Figure 2') and the Fig. 2 legend (1996, 1999, huge meningoencephalocele) match.

p. 393 ¶2 and ¶6 and Table 1 footnotes * and † match: nothing at presentation; 2 orbital infections with pseudotumour and 1 S. aureus lung abscess during follow-up, all resolved with antibiotics; 15 of 17 cultures positive.

results.corrected_extracted: At presentation, lesions against Wegener granulomatosis: fever 0 of 18 against 13 of 21, weight loss 0 against 7, arthralgia or arthritis 0 against 7, lung involvement 0 against 12, ear involvement 0 against 7; haemoglobin 14.2 against 11.1 g/dL; CRP 12.2 ± 12 against 79.4 ± 73.7 mg/L, p = 0.002; ESR 31 ± 25 against 66 ± 41 mm/h, p = 0.009 (the table does not say whether ± is the SD). In the lesion group CRP was abnormal in 9 and ESR in 8 of 18, white cells raised in 5 and anaemia present in 2; liver and kidney tests were normal and hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV tests negative in all. All 21 with Wegener granulomatosis had crusting, 3 a septal perforation on examination, and none involvement of the turbinates, lateral wall or palate; systemic symptoms and blood changes were absent in only 2 of them.

results.corrected_extracted: 44 biopsies from the 18 people with lesions (1 to 16 per person) and 29 from the 21 with Wegener granulomatosis: nonspecific changes in 19 of 44 against 7 of 29; among biopsies with significant abnormalities (25 and 22), perivenulitis 24 against 22, microabscesses in vessel walls 10 against 11, thrombi 7 against 5, leukocytoclastic vasculitis 7 against 14 (p = 0.02 per biopsy; per person 6 of 18 against 9 of 21, printed p = 0.11, editors' Fisher exact test p = 0.74), single giant cells or granulomas 0 against 9 and deeply located necrosis 0 against 19 (both p < 0.001). These extravascular changes were the only features found only in Wegener granulomatosis.

Discussion ¶7 (pp. 6–7) and Conclusions ¶1 match each limitation; not overstated. The authors add that fatal overdoses are unlikely to differ by cohort, since overdoses occurred at similar rates (p. 6).

Discussion ¶4–5 (p. 5): 'two to three times higher' citing ref. 29 (Sordo 2017, mortality meta-analysis, p. 8) with no figures; 5%–7.5% annual rate after a past-year overdose (ref. 2); insufficient power, hedged with 'may'.

key_findings.correction: All came for longstanding symptoms including nasal obstruction, nosebleeds and severe facial pain. At the first visit the commonest findings were diffuse necrotising ulcers, extensive crusting and septal perforation; destruction of the septum and inferior turbinates was found clinically in all, extending in more severe cases to the middle and superior turbinates and lateral nasal wall, which was entirely absorbed in 3. Palatal perforations were present in 2 people at the first visit and appeared during follow-up in 3 more; the authors say the lesions gave rise to difficulty swallowing and nasal reflux (numbers not given).

reporting_issues.correction: issue: Figure 3 gives the CIMDL group septum 100%, inferior turbinate 61%, middle turbinate 33%, superior turbinate 16%, lateral wall 11% and floor or palate 28%, which do not match the imaging counts in the text and Table 3 (75%, 62.5%, 12.5%, 31.25% and 25% of 16) or the clinical statement that the inferior turbinates were destroyed in all; the values are close to counts of 11, 6, 3, 2 and 5 of 18, of which only the 28% matches a stated count (palate perforations in 5 of 18 at the first visit or during follow-up, p. 393); the rest are not explained. | consequence: The figure understates inferior and middle turbinate and lateral wall involvement relative to the text (and slightly overstates the superior turbinate); claims should use the text and Table 3 with their denominator of 16.

issue: Table 2 shows that two C-ANCA-positive WG sera (WG 7 and WG 8, both positive on HMC-1/PR3 immunofluorescence) were negative in the PR3 capture ELISA: 2 of the 13 C-ANCA-positive WG sera tested by that assay (editors' count; 18 WG sera were tested by it in all); the discussion contrasts the 2 of 5 capture-negative C-ANCA sera in the CIMDL group with a literature figure of under 5% in WG without mentioning its own controls. | consequence: In this sample, capture-ELISA negativity did not clearly separate the groups (editors' Fisher exact test, 2 of 5 against 2 of 13, p = 0.53).

risk_of_bias.note: Design case series, JBI prevalence items as the round directs, overall high for frequency use: agree. Domain notes reproduce (CT: 7 studies in 5 people but 'two of 5 CT studies'; sex Fisher p = 0.53; per-person vasculitis p = 0.74; Wilson intervals). The paper never says 'retrospective' (design_detail), and Table 1 does not define ± (demographics say SD).

interpretation_gap.note: Minor is right. In 'claimed', the capture-ELISA comparison should read 2 of the 13 C-ANCA-positive WG sera tested by that assay (18 WG sera were tested in all).

missed: All biopsies were negative for infectious organisms, birefringent foreign material and Epstein-Barr virus, and nuclear atypia was absent (pp. 397–398): relevant to the adulterant and lymphoma questions.
The C-ANCA of the 5 CIMDL people had immunofluorescence patterns, titres and ELISA units as high as in WG (p. 394), which is why routine testing misleads.
Radiographic otitis media in 1 CIMDL against 5 WG people (31.25%, not significant), and general MR mucosal signal changes not significantly different between groups (p. 396).

key_findings.correction: The discussion states that overdose rates after stopping were about two to three times those observed in a general sample of people with opioid use disorder (reference 29), giving no figures for that comparison, and that the overdose rate in the sample lay within an approximate annual rate of 5% to 7.5% for subsequent overdoses reported for people with a past-year overdose (reference 2).

risk_of_bias.note: Retrospective cohort, ROBINS-I, overall serious: agree; selection after the start of follow-up (6 months enrolled after stopping) and the 30.5% excluded justify the serious domains. Figure 3 bars re-measured at 600 dpi: 25.9, 25.2, 23.0, 19.2%, weighted mean about 24.5%.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor is defensible: results are reported accurately and causation is disclaimed; the largest gap is the unsupported 'demonstrating ... two to three times higher' sentence (p. 5), which the card already flags.

missed: A psychiatric diagnosis went with higher adjusted odds of all four outcomes (admissions 1.56, emergency visits 1.49, overdose 1.61, opioid prescriptions 1.58; Table 2), the basis of the authors' 'especially among patients with comorbid mental illness' (PDF pp. 5, 7).
Women had lower odds of overdose but higher odds of emergency visits (1.16, 1.06–1.27) and opioid prescriptions (1.39, 1.25–1.54) (Table 2).
